newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ First pivotal to election victory - analysts.
newsitem.headline: NZ First pivotal to election victory - analysts.

text.p: New Zealand's first general election under a proportional voting system has not clearly produced a victory for the right or the left, political commentators on a TV3 panel said on Saturday.
"It would be lovely to be able to say that it is a victory for one or the other," said Auckland political scientist Raymond Miller.

"The thing is, we're talking about a centre party here in New Zealand First. Many supporters of New Zealand First would consider themselves to be more with Labour and the Alliance if they had to make a jump, others would consider themselves more

Latest vote counting shows the ruling conservative National Party with around 44 seats in parliament, plus another nine seats from its potential coalition partner Act New Zealand and its current partner United New Zealand.

The main opposition Labour party had around 37 seats. It is seen as likely to attract support on matters of confidence from the left-wing Alliance, which had around 13 seats. The Alliance ruled out a formal coalition with any other party unless negotiations took place before the election.

Winston Peters' New Zealand First party was projected by TV3 to receive around 17 seats, and the analysts said although NZ First was more likely to enter a coalition with Labour, it had not ruled out moving to the right.

"I think perhaps it's a bit glib for us to simply say it's a victory for one as against the other, when in fact here is this pivotal party in the middle, drawing from both extremes," said political commentator and editor of NZ Political Review Chris Trotter.

"It's a pivotal party born out of the right, not out of the left, and it will be able to extract concessions on matters like health and education from the National party which will not fundamentally undermine National's programme," Trotter said.
He suggested New Zealand First may not jump either way.

"I'm not sure that Winston will be able to do a deal with National. I'm not sure he'll want to in the end. He may simply keep his troops out of all battles, and out of all alliances, and vote within the parliament itself," Trotter said.
"Which means that it's Mr Bolger for prime minister for the next three years."
